claude.sample_unit: manually abstracted clinical notes (from 355 pregnant patients)

links.outcome: FPR and FNR differences across age, race, ethnicity subgroups for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5
links.effect: Differences in FPR/FNR observed between all groups, but 95% CIs overlapped except where n<5, suggesting differences not significant; larger sample needed.
links.quote: We did observe differences in FPR and FNR between all of the groups within the 3 demographic categories.

links.outcome: Hallucinated evidence in GPT-4 responses when verbatim evidence was required
links.effect: No hallucinated evidence found in any reviewed GPT-4 responses; GPT-3.5 sometimes used prompt text as evidence on blank notes.
links.quote: However, the researchers found no instances of hallucinated evidence in any of the GPT-4 responses that were reviewed, suggesting that requiring verbatim evidence from LLMs can be a solution to hallucinated responses.

links.outcome: Whether requiring verbatim evidence and justification reduces hallucination and omitted context
links.effect: GPT-4 evidence similar or identical to manual abstractors in most cases; no hallucinations observed in GPT-4 output.
links.quote: Our work also suggests that requiring the LLM to provide verbatim evidence and justification from the original text can help reduce the risk that relevant context about housing information is omitted from LLM results.

links.outcome: LLM recall and precision versus adjudicated manual labels for housing instability
links.effect: GPT-4 recall 0.924 vs manual 0.702, precision 0.850 vs manual 0.971; GPT-3.5 recall 0.717, precision 0.759.
links.quote: For current and past housing instability, the recall of GPT-4 was higher (0.924) than that of GPT-3.5 (0.717), RegEx (0.649), and manual abstraction (0.702).

links.outcome: Comparison of GPT-4, GPT-3.5, NER model, RegEx and manual abstraction on same notes
links.effect: GPT-4 had highest performance among automated methods with higher recall than humans (0.924 vs 0.702) but lower precision (0.850 vs 0.971).
links.quote: GPT-4 outperformed GPT-3.5, JSL, and RegEx in identifying patients experiencing current or past housing instability.

links.outcome: GPT-4 performance on deidentified versus original notes
links.effect: Recall dropped and precision rose on deidentified notes (current instability recall 0.906 original vs 0.812 complete de-id, 0.834 de-id except date).
links.quote: We found that in all cases, recall dropped but precision increased for the deidentified notes compared with the original notes ( Multimedia Appendix 2 and Table S18 in Multimedia Appendix 1 ).

links.outcome: Reproducibility of GPT output across runs
links.effect: GPT-4 results differ slightly each run, explaining small performance differences; nondeterminism was not tested formally.
links.quote: These minor increases in precision are likely because results from GPT-4 are slightly different each time the model is run, resulting in slight differences in performance.

links.outcome: Lower precision of LLM abstraction and need for human review
links.effect: GPT-4 precision (0.850) lower than human abstractors (0.971); authors state human review essential before patient engagement or care decisions.
links.quote: However, given the sensitive nature of housing insecurity and complexity of individual situations, final human review would be essential for any decision regarding patient communication or patient care.

Deidentifying notes before LLM processing and its effect on accuracy
Processing PHI within secure institutional cloud environment

links.outcome: Reference-label ambiguity
links.effect: 25% (103/415) dual abstraction; Cohen k coefficient 0.589, moderate agreement.
links.quote: Before adjudication, dually abstracted notes had a Cohen k coefficient of 0.589, which reflects moderate agreement [ 40 ] and highlights the ambiguity and subjectivity of abstracting complex concepts such as housing instability compared with other SDOH mentions such as employment or parental status, despite the abstractors having been trained on the same guidelines (see Supplementary Methods in Multimedia Appendix 1 ).

links.outcome: Performance on deidentified inputs
links.effect: Current-instability recall dropped from 0.906 to 0.812 complete de-id and 0.834 de-id except date.
links.quote: For example, for the notes labeled as current housing instability , the recall for GPT-4 on the original notes was 0.906, but this dropped to 0.812 and 0.834 for the complete de-id and de-id except date notes, respectively.

links.outcome: GPT-4 versus human abstraction
links.effect: GPT-4 recall 0.924 vs human 0.702; precision lower 0.850 vs human 0.971.
links.quote: Compared with GPT-3.5 and the named entity recognition model, GPT-4 had the highest performance and had a much higher recall (0.924) than human abstractors (0.702) in identifying patients experiencing current or past housing instability, although precision was lower (0.850) compared with human abstractors (0.971).

links.outcome: Subgroup FPR/FNR differences
links.effect: Differences observed, but 95% CIs overlapped for all groups except n<5 cases.
links.quote: However, when we examined the overlap of the 95% CIs between groups, we found that in all cases, except in cases where the sample sizes were extremely small (n<5), there was overlap between CIs for all the groups, suggesting that the differences between groups are not significant.

links.outcome: Prompt-text evidence misuse
links.effect: GPT-3.5 used prompt sentences as evidence and flagged current or past instability in several cases.
links.quote: In several cases, GPT-3.5 used sentences from the prompt text as evidence and justification and flagged the note as current or past instability.

links.outcome: Verbatim evidence requirement
links.effect: Reviewed GPT-4 responses had no hallucinated evidence when verbatim evidence was required.
links.quote: However, the researchers found no instances of hallucinated evidence in any of the GPT-4 responses that were reviewed, suggesting that requiring verbatim evidence from LLMs can be a solution to hallucinated responses.

links.outcome: AI abstraction precision
links.effect: Precision: GPT-4 0.850, GPT-3.5 0.759, RegEx 0.632 vs manual 0.971.
links.quote: However, manual abstraction had the highest precision among the 4 methods (0.971), compared with GPT-4 (0.850), GPT-3.5 (0.759), and RegEx (0.632).

links.outcome: algorithmic bias across age, race, and ethnic groups
links.effect: Differences in FPR and FNR between groups were not statistically significant based on overlapping 95% CIs across age, race, and ethnic categories, except in subgroups where sample sizes were under 5.
links.quote: However, when we examined the overlap of the 95% CIs between groups, we found that in all cases, except in cases where the sample sizes were extremely small (n<5), there was overlap between CIs for all the groups, suggesting that the differences between groups are not significant.
